Directly relevant to the ABYSSAL subagent: grants 4 bonus points (5 if character starts with permanent Resonance) for a deepened Abyssal Curse where Resonance resets to 0 (instead of causing a Resonance Break) upon exceeding 10, converting the overflow into a point of permanent Resonance (capped at the character's Essence rating); removable via 5 XP + a Harrowing in the Labyrinth (E:Ab p. 148). Also defines a parallel Ghost-only variant using tainted Passions/Whisper of Oblivion (E:Ab p. 284) instead of Resonance -- likely not relevant to any of the 5 playable splats but documented for completeness since Ghosts may appear as antagonists/NPCs.

name: Throwback
cost: Variable point Flaw, Celestial Exalted only
summary: LUNAR-RELEVANT FLAW: an Exalt with this Flaw harbors impulses and personality fragments from a previous incarnation of his Essence, giving his Essence its own distinct Nature; strong situational pulls require a Willpower roll (difficulty = Essence) to resist, and if permanent Willpower is ever exceeded by Essence, the Throwback Nature takes over entirely. Scales 1 pt. (merely inconvenient vestigial personality) to 5 pts. (outright malignant/insane remnant); Storytellers may interpolate 2- and 4-point versions.
mechanics: An Exalt with this Flaw harbors impulses and personality fragments from a previous incarnation of his Essence. In effect, his Essence has its own different Nature. If the Exalt finds himself in a situation where this Nature would feel strongly and desire a particular course of action, his player must roll Willpower against a difficulty of the Exalt's own Essence rating. If the roll fails, the character acts according to his Essence Nature, but does not regain Willpower for fulfilling its impulses. A botch means the Essence Nature takes over for the rest of the scene, replacing the character's normal personality and pattern of behavior. While "possessed" by the echoes of their former selves, Exalted regain Willpower according to the Nature of their Essence (see Exalted, p. 148). If a character with this Flaw ever has an Essence rating in excess of his permanent Willpower, his Nature changes entirely to the dictates of the Throwback. The value of this Flaw depends on the degree of deviation and malice of the former self. For one point, the vestigial personality is merely inconvenient, such as a Hedonist inside a stoic Paragon (or vice versa). A three-point Throwback is more alien and dangerous, exerting love toward half-remembered ancients and reincarnations of past associates -- or remembering feuds too bloody to end with death. Five-point versions of this Flaw are outright malignant or insane: remnants of demented god-kings steeped in their own arrogance and power. Their voice is an unceasing monologue of temptation and inhumanity that refuses to accept silence or death. Storytellers may interpolate the two- and four-point versions of this Flaw if so desired. Deathknights loyal to their masters may harbor an echo of Solar glory driving them to Resonance and punishment even as it guides them toward elusive redemption, though such a Throwback is never worth more than three points. Abyssal Exalted actively rebelling against their destiny gain no points for a heroic Throwback but may harbor a wicked personality like other Exalted and profit from it.
compatibility: RESTRICTED to Celestial Exalted by its own header ("Celestial Exalted only"): Solar, Lunar, Sidereal. Lunars are fully eligible at any point tier (1-5, with Storytellers able to interpolate 2 and 4). The text also separately extends a special-cased version to Abyssal deathknights (an echo of Solar glory pulling them toward redemption, capped at 3 points) and notes rebellious Abyssals gain no points for a heroic Throwback but may still take a wicked one -- an explicit exception carved out despite Abyssals not being 'Celestial Exalted.'
notes: DIRECTLY LUNAR-RELEVANT: as Celestial Exalted whose Essence passes to a new soul upon death (like Solars and Sidereals), a Lunar could take this Flaw to represent impulses/personality fragments bleeding through from whoever last carried her Essence -- thematically resonant with Lunar concerns about identity and past lives, similar to how Dark Fate (pg-flaw-dark-fate) notes Celestial Exalted pass dooms to their next incarnation. Same header-vs-body inconsistency as Permanent Caste Mark (pg-flaw-permanent-caste-mark) and Greater Curse (pg-flaw-greater-curse): header says "Celestial Exalted only" but the text explicitly carves out special rules for Abyssal deathknights (echo of Solar glory, capped 3 points) -- flag for the Abyssal subagent. No Sidereal-specific carve-out is mentioned beyond the general Celestial-Exalted eligibility.

name: Becoming the Wood Friend
summary: Terrestrial Circle spell that bonds the caster empathically to plant life, letting her move through dense foliage at full speed and become nearly untrackable until she next sleeps.
requirements: Prerequisite Charm: Terrestrial Circle Sorcery.
mechanics: Target: Caster. Until the caster next sleeps: she moves through even the densest foliage unhindered at top speed with no Athletics roll; forest, scrubland and cultivated fields count as open terrain for speed/fatigue purposes; no mundane tracking method can follow her (her scent becomes plant-like); supernatural trackers suffer a +2 difficulty to track her, and this sorcery overrides any Charm or effect that would otherwise make her easier to track. She adds her Essence to Strength for jumping/climbing through wooded terrain and to Dexterity for base movement speed in green environments, and adds Essence to other Athletics rolls made moving through or balancing on plant life. The bond runs both ways: the caster must succeed at a Willpower roll to knowingly do serious harm to a living plant or tree (cutting live wood, setting unprotected fires, joining a large-scale harvest); gathering fruit/nuts, collecting fallen wood, or pruning dead branches does not count. Committing such harm instantly ends the spell and locks the caster out of recasting it for three full days.
compatibility: Any Lunar Exalted (No Moon caste) who has learned Terrestrial Circle Sorcery. This is a generic Circle of Emerald (Terrestrial Circle) spell from Exalted: Savant and Sorcerer, not unique to Lunars.

name: Calling the Wind's Kiss
summary: Terrestrial Circle spell that conjures a magical wind to speed one sailing vessel's passage or to curse and hinder an enemy ship, out to a range scaling with the caster's Essence.
requirements: Prerequisite Charm: Terrestrial Circle Sorcery.
mechanics: Target: One sailing vessel within visual range, up to (permanent Essence x 3) miles away. Countered by countermagic or by casting Calling the Wind's Kiss in opposition; a spirit of the air with permanent Essence >= the caster's may seize control of the spell with a Willpower roll (difficulty = caster's permanent Essence); the caster can dismiss the spell at will unless a spirit has commandeered it.
cost: 10 motes + 2 motes per additional hour (maximum 20 additional motes)
compatibility: Any Lunar Exalted (No Moon caste) who has learned Terrestrial Circle Sorcery. This is a generic Circle of Emerald (Terrestrial Circle) spell from Exalted: Savant and Sorcerer, not unique to Lunars.

summary: Celestial Circle spell that magically enslaves a victim's heart into genuine, intelligent devotion to the caster, with only one chance per year for the victim to break free on the anniversary of her birth.
requirements: Prerequisite Charm: Celestial Circle Sorcery.
mechanics: Target: One creature (no effect on any creature with permanent Essence greater than the caster's). For 30 motes, ropes of light pierce and merge with the victim's Essence; mortals are affected instantly, while an Essence-using victim's player may make a reflexive Willpower roll (difficulty = caster's permanent Essence) to resist, and success makes that Essence-wielder immune to this spell from the same caster again. Rather than a mindless drone, the victim retains intelligence and asks clarifying questions but genuinely, sincerely loves and trusts the caster, rationalizing her devotion as real (often unaware she is enchanted, especially if bound while asleep); onlookers may recognize her as an ensorcelled puppet. Once a year, on her birthday, the victim's player may make a reflexive Willpower roll (difficulty = caster's permanent Essence) to break free permanently (and become immune to this spell from the same caster); failure resets the bond for another year with no memory of the attempt. Bound victims will cheerfully sacrifice themselves or loved ones if they believe it serves the caster's interests.

name: Wilderness Gem
summary: Level Four sample Hearthstone (Lunar Type): a gem that grants its bearer an instinctive knack for surviving in the wilderness, whatever the environment.
requirements: Manse Background (see manse-background-altered); attunement to the Manse that produced this Hearthstone.
mechanics: Trigger: none, constant. Gives the bearer instinctive knowledge of where safe shelter and campsites can be found, which plants and animals are safe to eat, and how to recognize the signs of the onset of dangerous weather. The gem adds four automatic successes to any Survival roll the bearer's player makes and lets the character take part in supernatural tracking contests.
compatibility: Any Lunar Exalted (No Moon caste) holding a Manse Background and attuned to a Manse that produces this Hearthstone. One of Savant and Sorcerer's own explicitly labeled 'sample' Hearthstones, not unique to Lunars or Lunars -- the 'Lunar' Type label describes the stone's Theme/flavor, not an eligibility restriction.

name: Gem of Life
summary: Level Five sample Hearthstone (Earth Type): a smooth, black, iridescent stone that grants its bearer the extended lifespan of a Celestial Exalt, halting aging and the infirmities of old age for as long as she holds it and remains attuned to its Manse.
requirements: Manse Background (see manse-background-altered); attunement to the Manse that produced this Hearthstone.
mechanics: Trigger: none, constant. The bearer does not age and does not suffer the infirmities and illnesses of old age, even if she was already old when she acquired the stone; she cannot die of old age or illness while bearing it, but can still be harmed and killed through other means. If she loses attunement to the Manse or stops bearing the Hearthstone, she resumes aging normally.
compatibility: Any Lunar Exalted (No Moon caste) holding a Manse Background and attuned to a Manse that produces this Hearthstone. One of Savant and Sorcerer's own explicitly labeled 'sample' Hearthstones; the source text's example specifically describes a Dragon-Blood bearer gaining a Celestial Exalt's lifespan, but nothing in the stone's description restricts its Trigger/Expression by the wearer's Exalt type, so it is inventoried as usable by any Exalt (including Sidereals) who holds it -- flagged here rather than assumed silently.

name: Home's Hearth
summary: Level Five sample Hearthstone (Sidereal Type): an irregular, multicolored gemstone that instantly teleports the bearer and up to five chosen companions to or from his Manse's Hearthroom from anywhere in Creation, notably used by all three of the Sidereals' hidden Manses.
requirements: Manse Background (see manse-background-altered); attunement to the Manse that produced this Hearthstone.
mechanics: Trigger: concentration. The bearer and up to five other people of his choice can instantly travel from anywhere in Creation to the Manse's Hearthroom, or leave the Hearthroom for a destination within 100 miles of the Manse; the transit is instantaneous and unaffected by distance or time. The effect is less reliable from the Wyld: the bearer's player must make a Wits + Occult roll to safely transport from the Wyld to the Manse. Failure drops the travelers into a random place within the Wyld, and a botch renders the stone useless for 48 hours while its Essence recharges.
compatibility: Any Lunar Exalted (No Moon caste) holding a Manse Background and attuned to a Manse that produces this Hearthstone. One of Savant and Sorcerer's own explicitly labeled 'sample' Hearthstones -- given the 'Sidereal' Type label (the book's own Hearthstone-Type taxonomy, unrelated to Exalt type) and the book's own note that all three of the Sidereals' hidden Manses use a Home's Hearth, this stone is not restricted to Sidereal Exalted and is equally usable by a Lunar bearing the right Manse.
notes: Chapter Three: Demesne and Manse, 'Sample Hearthstones' -> 'Level Five', printed pp. 70-71 (PDF 71-72). This is the last of Savant and Sorcerer's 15 sample Hearthstones (3 per level x 5 levels), closing out this book's illustrative Hearthstone catalog; the book itself notes this list is a guideline for Storytellers rather than an exhaustive catalog, and its own intro sidebar points to Book of Three Circles' Chapter Six 'long roll of Hearthstones' as the more comprehensive (and not superseded) catalog, reviewed separately in this same pass. name: Artifact Rating Framework (Power, Usefulness, Game Impact, Script Immunity, Drawback)
summary: GM-facing rules framework for rating any artifact on the standard five-dot Background scale by averaging four sub-ratings (Power, Usefulness, Game Impact, Script Immunity) and subtracting extra Drawback.
requirements: Storyteller/artificer-player collaboration; used whenever adjudicating an existing artifact's Background cost or designing a new one.
mechanics: Each aspect is rated 1-5 (Drawback is separate): Power measures raw effectiveness (bonus dice, Charm-duplication tier, up to Power 5 duplicating Essence 5-6 Charms including perfect effects, and N/A 'World-Shattering' artifacts that only lesser artifacts or legendary beings can resist); Usefulness measures how broadly applicable the item is, from Very Limited Use (••) up to Always Active (•••••), reduced by one or two dots for items usable only once or a limited number of times per story; Game Impact measures how much the artifact would disrupt the ongoing story/series, from None (•) to Changing (•••••); Script Immunity measures how protected from loss/destruction the item is by narrative convention, from None (•) to Total (•••••, enduring into the next Age). Weapons and armor use a simplified Power calculation: average the Resources cost of the mundane base item with the Power of any added abilities. To calculate final Artifact rating: add Power + Game Impact + Usefulness + Script Immunity, subtract any Drawback points taken above the minimum (which equals Power), then divide by four and round up.
compatibility: Storyteller and player tool for any Exalt designing, rating, or adjudicating an artifact; not a player-facing trait in itself.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Artifact Levels' -> 'Power'/'Usefulness'/'Game Impact'/'Script Immunity'/'Calculating the Artifact Rating', printed pp. 23-29 (PDF 24-30). Two worked examples (a Power •• daiklave, a Power •• mask) are given but not separately inventoried; the mask example matches the 'Mask' sample artifact inventoried below. Adapted for Lunar from this project's already-verified Exalted: The Sidereals transcription of this same universal cross-splat Savant and Sorcerer / Book of Three Circles content (docs/references/exalted1e/sidereal/inventory/exalted-the-sidereals.json); citation, mechanics, and cost re-verified unchanged since this is identical sourcebook text on the same page, with only Exalt-type framing in compatibility/notes updated for Lunar Exalted (No Moon caste sorcery access, Silver Pact culture).

name: Artifact Drawback Types and Alternate Power Sources
summary: GM-facing rules for the four Drawback subtypes (Essence, Component, Maintenance, Notoriety) that offset an artifact's cost, plus alternate ways to power an artifact besides direct Essence expenditure (Hearthstones, Essence Accumulators, Energy Taps, blood/life sacrifices).
requirements: Storyteller/artificer-player collaboration during artifact design or adjudication.
mechanics: Essence Drawback (X to +•••••) scales an artifact's mote requirement from normal up to 20x normal (Essence Glutton); reduced by installing a Hearthstone (lowers Drawback by the Hearthstone's level), an Essence Accumulator (a separate artifact acting like a Hearthstone of its own Artifact-rating level), an Energy Tap (built two Artifact levels below the Hearthstone-equivalence it grants, tied to a violent natural phenomenon like a volcano or whirlpool), or blood/life sacrifices (one health level of blood per use lowers Drawback by •, a mortal's life by ••, an Essence-wielder's death by •••). Component Drawback (X to •••••) scales the number of exotic ingredients required, from a trace of one Magical Material up to 10 rare exotic components. Maintenance Drawback requires Lore/Occult at least equal to its rating to service; unmaintained artifacts lose 10% speed/maneuverability, 2L/4B damage or soak, or one Power dot per 10 hours in arrears, persisting (and potentially becoming permanent) until repaired; large artifacts may need a repair team led by a Charisma + Presence roll (difficulty = team size / 3). Notoriety Drawback (X to •••••) scales how well-known and legally/socially fraught the artifact's possession is, from Unknown up to Anathema (feared and hunted by multiple powerful factions).
compatibility: Storyteller and player tool for any Exalt designing an artifact; not a player-facing trait in itself.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Drawback' -> 'Essence Drawback'/'Alternate Power Sources'/'Component Drawback'/'Notoriety Drawback'/'Maintenance Drawback', printed pp. 26-33 (PDF 27-34). The three Personal/Larger/Massive Artifact Attunement-and-Activation mote tables (printed p. 26/PDF 27) were not transcribed row-by-row; they set baseline Essence costs by Power level and artifact scale. name: Merit: Starting Workshop (variable-cost Merit)
summary: Variable-cost Merit granting the character an existing workshop at character creation: a 5-point version for unrestricted access to a Shogunate-era workshop, or a 10-point version for a First Age factory-cathedral.
requirements: Storyteller approval; may be vetoed if inappropriate to the game (e.g. frequently-traveling characters or low-powered games).
mechanics: 5 points: unrestricted access to a Shogunate-era workshop (+1 difficulty to artifact creation rolls; see artifact-creation-five-step-process). 10 points: access to a First Age factory-cathedral (+0 difficulty). Subtract 2 points from the cost if the character must sometimes go without access (no more than one season per year of unavailability); subtract 3 points if unavailable more than three seasons per year.
compatibility: Any Exalt with Storyteller approval; not restricted to a particular splat, though a Lunar more typically works at a remote, hidden forge under Luna's light rather than a fixed institutional workshop (see artifact-creation-lunar-notes).
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, sidebar within 'The Third Step: Components', printed pp. 32-33 (PDF 33-34). This is a discrete named Merit trait defined by this supplement; noted for completeness alongside this book's other named Merit (Moonsilver Initiate, merit-moonsilver-initiate) despite this inventory's earlier finding (see source-manifest.json rulesNotes) that the Exalted: The Sidereals core book itself has no Merits & Flaws chapter -- this supplement independently introduces a small number of standalone Merits rather than a full system. name: Merit: Moonsilver Initiate (5-pt Merit, 2-pt for Lunars)
summary: Merit representing that the character has earned or stolen the secrets of crafting moonsilver, letting her work this Magical Material despite it being jealously guarded by the Lunar Exalted's Silver Pact.
requirements: Storyteller approval.
mechanics: Grants the knowledge needed to forge moonsilver (see magical-materials-catalog for the forging ritual's requirements). Non-Lunar characters who let it become known that they work moonsilver, or who carry moonsilver artifacts, risk being challenged by Lunars even if the character has been accepted as a nain-ya by the Silver Pact.
compatibility: Any Exalt with Storyteller approval; most relevant to a non-Lunar PC in a Lunar-heavy game, since a Lunar character is already raised within Silver Pact moonsilver-working culture -- the book itself calls out the reduced 2-point cost for Lunar Exalted specifically. Carries an ongoing social-consequence Drawback (Silver Pact jealousy) rather than a mechanical restriction; see magical-materials-catalog for the moonsilver forging ritual itself and artifact-background-altered for how moonsilver ownership already works for Lunar PCs by default.

name: The Five Magical Materials (Jade, Soulsteel, Moonsilver, Starmetal, Orichalcum)
summary: Summary of this book's lore/forging notes for each of the Five Magical Materials, including the Sidereal-specific and grim account of how starmetal is actually produced (an audited, condemned minor god's Essence, executed and cast down to Creation for a Sidereal savant to collect).
mechanics: Jade: the only Magical Material forgeable by ordinary Terrestrial techniques (carving with diamond-tipped tools, since it cannot be hammered unless heavily alloyed with steel); its five colors each correspond to one of the five elements and can only augment Aspect Abilities/Charms of that element. Soulsteel: alloyed from Labyrinth ore and the souls of the dead via Craft (Soulforging); mortals need a Valor roll (difficulty 2, or 1 for Dragon-Blooded) just to touch a soulsteel artifact and suffer a die penalty using it (other Exalted are immune), and any living being of Essence 3 or less other than a Solar must make a Valor roll (difficulty 1) when facing a soulsteel weapon; soulsteel weapons gain +1 Accuracy and soulsteel armor grants two extra soak dice. Moonsilver: purified from Wyld chaos by Luna herself, now found almost exclusively in the Wyld; forging requires harvesting ore under moonlight with no crafted tools (Intelligence + Lore roll, difficulty 3), purification rituals known to No Moons (or learned by other Lunars over 6-minus-Essence years), and working only at night with unpolluted fuel and moonlight-only water; non-Lunars who wish to use moonsilver artifacts must pass trials akin to the Silver Pact's rites of passage (see merit-moonsilver-initiate). Starmetal: the rarest Magical Material, popularly said to be refined from a fallen star, but actually the Essence of a minor god condemned to death by the Bureau of Destiny's audit process (see Exalted: The Sidereals, pp. 34-40) and cast down for a Sidereal savant to collect and forge; once collected it can be worked with ordinary mundane tools like any other metal, and is especially prized for the pens Sidereals use to write prayers to the pattern spiders. Orichalcum: mined from deposits (heavily guarded since the Usurpation) or refined from natural gold via a lava-heated solar forge and mirror-focused sunlight (Intelligence + Craft [Orichalcum] roll, difficulty 3); it alone of the Five Magical Materials can embody perfection and suits any artifact purpose, destructive or restorative.
compatibility: Reference material underlying the Artifact Background and artifact-creation rules for any Exalt; the moonsilver entry is specifically relevant to Lunar-sourced artifacts and interacts directly with this splat's own Artifact Background alteration (see artifact-background-altered) and Moonsilver-Shaping Rite Charm (see moonsilver-shaping-rite).
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Ingredients of Wonder' -> 'Magical Materials' -> 'Jade'/'Soulsteel'/'Moonsilver'/'Starmetal'/'Orichalcum', printed pp. 37-40 (PDF 38-41). name: Making an Artifact: the Five-Step Creation Process
summary: GM-facing rules for player characters constructing a new artifact from scratch in the Age of Sorrows: prerequisites, the five-step process (Design, Tools and Assistants, Components, Construction, Finishing Up), and notes on assembly-line mass production of low-level items.
requirements: Craft •••, Lore ••• and Occult ••• minimum to attempt any artifact creation.
mechanics: Step One (Design): four methods -- Design from Existing Plans (Lore 4+ per Artifact level), Design from Reconstruction (Intelligence + Investigation research through ruins/libraries, difficulty = Artifact rating + 2, 3+ successes per level), Design from Existing Example (Intelligence + Occult to study or disassemble an existing artifact, difficulty = rating + 3, botching disassembly causes an explosion dealing 10L per Artifact level), or Design from First Principles (three parallel Intelligence + Lore/Occult/Craft rolls, difficulty = rating + 4, 5 successes per level each). Step Two (Tools and Assistants): workshop quality reduces difficulty (basic +4/+3 to base difficulty depending on tools, advanced workshop +2, Shogunate-era +1, First Age +0), plus bonuses for assistants (thaumaturges, Terrestrial or Celestial Exalted artisans, summoned demons/elementals scaled via the Scope system); the Merit: Starting Workshop and the 'Workshops of Creation' survey of notable real-world workshops (Heptagram, Lookshy, the Great Houses, Yu-Shan, the Deathlords) are covered as separate rows/notes. Step Three (Components): most artifacts need only a scrap of a Magical Material; more exotic components scale with the desired Artifact rating (typically the artifact's rating minus one). Step Four (Construction): a series of Intelligence + Craft rolls (one per season) accumulating successes per an Artifact-Level-to-Base-Difficulty-and-Successes-Required table (Level 1: difficulty 3/10 successes, up to Level 5: difficulty 7/250 successes); the maker commits Essence equal to the Artifact rating throughout, forfeiting the artifact if withdrawn, and botches trigger escalating catastrophes (destroyed components, lost progress, design flaws, Essence-bound fate, or explosions). Step Five (Finishing Up): committed Essence returns on completion; repeating a similar item reduces required successes by 5 per repetition (to a floor). Mass production of Artifact • (and sometimes ••) items is possible via an assembly line: halve the item's Resources cost through enough prototypes, then succeed at an Intelligence + Lore roll (difficulty = rating + 2) to build a production station (cost = rating + 3 Resources per station, rating + 2 Resources per season to maintain) that lets mortal thaumaturges enchant items via Intelligence + Craft rolls.
compatibility: Any Exalt (or, for some steps, cooperating groups of Exalted/mortals) attempting to build a new artifact.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Making an Artifact' -> 'The First Step: Design' through 'The Fifth Step: Finishing Up' plus 'In-Game Creation' introduction, printed pp. 29-34 (PDF 30-35). The detailed Workshop-difficulty/assistant-bonus tables and the 'Workshops of Creation' setting survey (printed p. 33/PDF 34) were paraphrased rather than transcribed table-row-by-row. name: In-Game Creation: the Lunar Exalted
summary: Lunar-specific artifact-creation notes: unlike the Terrestrial or Sidereal Exalted, Lunars never worked in coordinated production teams; First Age Lunars crafted at remote forges under Luna's blessing, benefiting from their Solar consorts' peace and security and from moonsilver's greater First Age abundance, while modern Lunars work in secret, isolated locations close to the Wyld, pouring personal Essence (and often their own blood) into deeply individual, non-mass-produced pieces.
requirements: Lunar Exalted attempting artifact creation; interacts with the standard five-step process (see artifact-creation-five-step-process).
mechanics: Lunars never really worked together in coordinated groups or with consistent outside assistance the way Terrestrials do, but First Age Lunar artificers benefited from the resources of their Solar consorts and the peace and security in which to craft the weapons and items they needed; moonsilver, the metal sacred to Luna, was also far easier to find in the First Age than it is now, when it exists almost exclusively in the Wyld. During the Solar Deliberative, Lunars worked at forges in remote locations, asking Luna's blessing as they used simple tools to work their ingredients together; this was a violent process, often requiring the Exalt to give up her own blood to perfect the item. There was no mass production -- every work, every piece, was important, and every piece carried a little of the spirit of its creator with it. Gifts of these artifacts were given out of deep respect or love, and misuse of such a gift was sure to draw the Lunar's anger. After the Lunar Exalted fled the Realm following the Usurpation, they brought the secret of working moonsilver with them, and with Luna's blessing they kept it safe even as many of their kind went mad in the Wyld. Now, Lunar artificers work in secret places close to the Wyld that both threatens them and gives them security and power, pouring their hearts, souls, and Essence into each piece of work, jealously guarding the secrets of moonsilver and designing personal works for both war and survival at crude forges under the bright light of Luna. As ever, Lunar artifacts are not works of whimsy or toys -- they are often beautiful works of art, but always practical, and often carry a razor-sharp purpose hidden beneath their eye-catching quicksilver glory.
compatibility: Lunar Exalted specifically; this section exists as this splat's counterpart to the chapter's per-Exalt-type 'In-Game Creation' notes for the Terrestrial, Sidereal, Abyssal, and Solar Exalted (not independently inventoried here, as out of scope for this splat's own pass).
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'In-Game Creation' -> 'The Lunar Exalted', printed pp. 35-36 (PDF 36-37), immediately following 'The Sidereal Exalted' and preceding 'The Abyssal Exalted'/'The Solar Exalted'. This row was read directly from the source PDF for this Lunar-specific pass rather than adapted from the Sidereal or Abyssal inventory files, since neither transcribed this splat-specific subsection (each covered only its own Exalt type's entry in this same per-splat survey).

name: Exotic Ingredients: First Age and Age of Sorrows Examples
summary: Two GM-facing sample lists of setting-flavored exotic ingredients an artificer might use to seed an artifact's Essence pattern: five First Age examples (mostly synthesized/conjured) and ten Age of Sorrows examples (mostly gruesome trophies and salvage), each with a brief mechanical hook.
mechanics: Five First Age examples: distorted Half-Damned blood (for devices delving beyond Creation or penetrating demons' defenses); elemental salt-diamonds (removes an artifact's otherwise-unavoidable Drawback); a mortal warrior's perfect-strike kata etched and traced onto weapons (+2 dice to wielders' Melee attack pools); a compressed dragon-track/Demesne rod (lets an artifact draw Essence directly from a Demesne without a Manse or Hearthstone); spiritual drilling rigs into the Labyrinth (all destroyed in the Contagion). Ten Age of Sorrows examples: ground dust of broken artifacts (-2 to a similar item's construction difficulty); vented failed/wild Hearthstones (-•• Essence Drawback); Fair Folk blood-flowers mixed with the artificer's blood (infuses a Virtue rated 4+ into the item for a related passive benefit); a god's eyes (potent Essence source, legally fraught to obtain); a thread from a Maiden's robe (aids artifacts under that Maiden's colleges); a Solar's own bones (necromantic feedback loop, draws Deathlord attention); dragon's blood (81 drops, potent but hazardous to harvest); distilled Heavenly Quintessence/Ambrosia; Wyld constrained in moonsilver chalices (forced into complementary shapes near an unfinished artifact); and lightning-fused desert obsidian (used by the artificers of Gem).
compatibility: Storyteller/artificer-player tool for flavoring new artifact designs for any Exalt, including Sidereals.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Exotic Ingredients' -> 'Five Sample Exotic Ingredients Used in the First Age' / 'Ten Exotic Ingredients Used in the Age of Sorrows', printed pp. 40-41 (PDF 41-42). name: Collar of Dawn's Cleansing Light (Artifact •)
summary: Level One sample artifact: a piece of neck jewelry (collar, choker, torc, or delicate necklace) that keeps its wearer immaculately clean and bolsters her resistance to disease and poison, common enough that many Dragon-Blooded wear one simply to show off.
requirements: Attunement (1 mote of Essence).
mechanics: Negates all Social-roll penalties for being dirty or unkempt, regardless of actual conditions (the wearer could live under a rubbish heap for weeks and emerge as if freshly groomed for a ball). Once attuned, the cleansing effect extends beyond clothing to the wearer's own body, and its light adds two dice to Resistance rolls against disease or poison. Crafted from any of the Five Magical Materials, including soulsteel.
compatibility: Any Exalt; explicitly noted as popular among Dragon-Blooded for status display as much as utility.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Collar of Dawn's Cleansing Light', printed pp. 40-41 (PDF 41-42). name: Mask (Artifact ••)
summary: Level Two sample artifact: a plain ivory face mask that lets an Exalt alter her appearance to look like anyone she wishes and fully control the emotions her face shows, a fixture of Exalted political and emotional intrigue since the First Age.
requirements: Attunement (5 motes of Essence, the normal cost for a Level •• item).
mechanics: Adds four dice to the wearer's Intelligence + Larceny pool for any disguise attempt (see core Exalted, p. 255). Once attuned, also grants an extra four dice to any attempt to misdirect others about the wearer's true motives, such as relevant Presence, Socialize, or Bureaucracy rolls.
compatibility: Any Exalt; this is the same sample item used as this chapter's Power/Game-Impact worked example (see artifact-creation-rating-framework), where the book calls out its disguise trick as unreliable against a Sidereal's foresight ('a child's toy to Sidereals') -- a caution equally worth a Lunar player's attention when weighing how much to trust a Mask's disguise against a canny or Celestially-touched opponent.

name: Ring of Being (Artifact ••••)
summary: Level Four sample artifact: one of a small number of rings forged by the legendary Twilight artificer Jervon, each a pure and perfect representation of its Magical Material, that renders its wearer's innate form and mind untouchable by magic, spirits, the Wyld, or demonic influence.
requirements: Attunement (15 motes of Essence); the Exalt can only attune to a ring made of her own kind's appropriate Magical Material (e.g. a Lunar gains no benefit from a jade ring beyond its beauty). No known soulsteel Rings of Being exist -- the secret of making one was lost before the Deathlords rose.
mechanics: While attuned, no magic or power of the dead, the Fair Folk, demons, spirits, or the Wyld can alter the wearer's innate form or mind: she can still be harmed by physical attacks or effects, but no spirit's Charms, no Wyld chaos, no spell can addle her mind or compel her love, and no demon can claim her soul. The exact non-Magical-Material ingredients needed to forge one (at least a sample of the Deep Wyld and possibly a fragment of the Labyrinth) are only partially recorded.
compatibility: Any Exalt, restricted to a ring forged from that Exalt-type's own appropriate Magical Material (a documented orichalcum example was worn by the Solar Deliberative's Hierophant; other Magical-Material versions are rumored to have gone to Lunar, Sidereal, and Terrestrial Exalted).
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Ring of Being', printed pp. 41-42 (PDF 42-43). name: Wings of the Raptor (Artifact ••••)
summary: Level Four sample artifact: a heavy cloak, first built by an earthbound Solar to join his Lunar love in flight, that transforms into a 20-foot wingspan granting true flight along with enhanced aerial combat and sight.
requirements: Attunement (10 motes of Essence to transform from cloak to wings; the spent Essence cannot be reclaimed until the wings revert to their mundane cloak form).
mechanics: While flying: moves at five times the wearer's base running speed (80 mph); adds six dice to Dexterity rolls involving aerial maneuvering, including dodging and hand-to-hand combat; adds six dice to sight-based Perception rolls and reduces distance penalties by three. A flying character can only be attacked in hand-to-hand combat during the initiative tick when she herself attacks in hand-to-hand combat; opponents who want to reach her outside that tick must reflexively close to hand-to-hand range at a -3 penalty (-1 for long weapons like spears), while she may attack or counterattack freely. Ranged attacks against a flying wearer are unaffected by this restriction.
compatibility: Any Exalt.

name: Soul Mirror (Artifact •••••)
summary: Level Five sample artifact: a soulsteel grand daiklave forged for the Lover Clad in Raiment of Tears' champion, lost after her nemissary fell to two Dragon-Blooded martial artists, that drains Essence and Willpower on every hit and traps the souls of those it kills.
requirements: Attunement (the same Essence cost as an ordinary grand daiklave; see core Exalted, p. 342); all other statistics match a mundane grand daiklave except for an additional (fourth) Hearthstone setting on the handle.
mechanics: On a successful hit, drains one point of the target's temporary Willpower and a number of motes of Essence equal to the wielder's permanent Essence (half, rounded down, passes to the wielder; the rest is consumed by the sword). Anyone the blade kills has their ghost drawn into Soul Mirror instead of the Underworld or Lethe, visible tormented in the flat blade until consumed; the wielder may consume a trapped soul at any time to add 1 to the weapon's speed, accuracy, and damage for seven days (up to four consumed souls' benefits active at once). Any player whose character faces Soul Mirror in battle must succeed at a Willpower roll (difficulty 4 for mortals, 3 for Exalted/other magical beings, 2 for Solars or Abyssals) or suffer a four-die penalty to attack rolls. As a reflexive action costing one contained soul and all of the wielder's remaining peripheral Essence (requires at least 10 Essence in the peripheral pool), the wielder may negate any single attack that would drop her to Incapacitated or below, triggering an anima flare, healing all lethal/bashing damage from that strike, and healing aggravated damage equal to her permanent Essence.
compatibility: Any Exalt capable of wielding a grand daiklave; currently lost, its location unknown.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, 'Sample Artifacts' -> 'Soul Mirror', printed pp. 43-44 (PDF 44-45). name: Warstriders: History, Appearance, and the Five Design Classes
summary: GM/lore-facing overview of warstriders as a category of First Age/Shogunate/modern siege armor: their history from the Solar Deliberative through the Usurpation and Contagion to the Age of Sorrows, the three broad design eras (First Age, Shogunate, Modern), and the five basic design classes (Scout, Common, Noble, Royal, Juggernaut).
mechanics: Warstriders are giant powered suits of armor, 16 to 30 feet tall, worn rather than piloted like a vehicle. Only three Age-of-Sorrows factions field them extensively: the Realm's legions, Lookshy's Seventh Legion, and the Deathlords' armies; the standard deployment unit is the 'fang' (five warstriders plus supporting infantry/officers, totaling talon size). Sidereals historically made the least use of warstriders of any Exalt type -- starmetal scarcity meant only a handful were ever built, nearly all First Age manufacture, carefully hidden before the Usurpation and rarely deployed since (see artifact-creation-sidereal-notes for related starmetal-scarcity lore). Design classes, by era: First Age warstriders were individualistic and ornamental, experimenting with built-in weapons/devices; Shogunate designs were utilitarian and regimented, with lesser versions of First Age weaponry; Modern warstriders (post-Contagion) are often mismatched assemblages of salvaged parts, usually lacking First Age Essence weapons. The five basic classes (statted in warstrider-scout/-common/-noble/-royal/-juggernaut below) emerged from First Age battlefield experimentation and remain the standard typology used in the Age of Sorrows.
compatibility: Storyteller/setting reference for any Exalt encountering or discussing warstriders; not itself a player-selectable trait. Lunar-specific deployment notes are called out because they bear on how a Lunar PC would plausibly acquire one -- Lunars are not a major warstrider-fielding faction (the Realm's legions, Lookshy's Seventh Legion, and the Deathlords field them extensively; Lunars do not), but per this appendix's own 'Basic Warstrider Designs' notes, Lunars are one of the few Exalt types explicitly attested to have piloted Royal-class warstriders in the First Age (see warstrider-royal).
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, unheaded introduction plus 'Appearance' -> 'First Age'/'Shogunate'/'Modern', 'Operation' intro, 'Deployment in the Second Age' -> 'The Realm'/'Lookshy'/'The Deathlords'/'Others', and 'Classes of Warstriders' intro, printed pp. 144-149 (PDF 145-150). The 'Too Many Warstriders!' Storyteller sidebar (printed p. 148/PDF 149, on tuning per-legion deployment density) is summarized here rather than separately inventoried, as a pure Storyteller-tuning note with no player-facing content. name: Wearing a Warstrider: Operation, Attunement, and Essence Costs
summary: GM-facing mechanical rules for how a character straps into and operates a warstrider: familiarization time, the attunement/Hearthstone-power link, low-power stance, and which kinds of beings (spirits, the dead, the Fair Folk, mortals/God-Blooded) can use one and under what restrictions.
requirements: Ability to channel and commit Essence to artifacts; a warstrider additionally requires a Hearthstone (usually from a level-three Manse) to operate at full power.
mechanics: Familiarization requires no roll but takes (10 - permanent Essence) days to learn to optimize attunement and move well in the control system. Attunement costs 10 motes of Essence in most cases (more for some First Age-weapon-equipped suits) and takes about five minutes to establish or fade, mirroring the time needed to don/remove the armor; while attuned, damage that breaches the armor also harms the wearer via feedback. A warstrider drains its mounted Hearthstone entirely to power itself (the wearer gains no personal benefit from that stone while it's installed); lacking a Hearthstone, a wearer can self-power the suit at 5 motes + 1 Willpower per turn plus 1 mote per action (including movement), though most Second Age warstriders aren't built to sustain this long. Low-power stance (six minus permanent Essence turns to toggle, with proper Hearthstone) cuts maintenance accrual to one-third rate, allows a Hearthstone one level lower, halves movement, halves weapon speed/rate, adds two successes to the already-existing small-target attack penalty, subtracts two dice from attacks/dodges/parries, and reduces initiative by 5. Spirits with a warstrider as part of their panoply can materialize already attuned. The dead pay double Essence commitment to attune to non-soulsteel warstriders and can only use them while materialized or animating a corpse; hungry ghosts generally lack the discipline to operate one. The Fair Folk do not use warstriders by disposition, though an individual fae could choose to. Mortals/God-Blooded with the appropriate Merits (Exalted Players Guide) can attune using normal rules, limited mainly by their scant Essence and lack of penalty-reducing Charms.
compatibility: Any Exalt (or qualifying spirit, ghost, Fair Folk, mortal, or God-Blooded) who can attune to artifacts and gains access to a warstrider and its required Hearthstone.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Operation' -> body text, 'Essence Costs', 'Low-Power Stance', and 'Wearing Warstriders' (including the 'Stealth and Camouflage' sidebar on general adaptive-camouflage/mundane-camouflage rules, printed pp. 152-153/PDF 153-154, which is a general Stealth-rules digression rather than warstrider-specific and is summarized rather than separately inventoried), printed pp. 146, 150-153 (PDF 147, 151-154). name: Warstrider Benefits and Limitations (Strength, Armor, Size, Vision, Manipulation, Stealth)
summary: GM-facing summary of the mechanical upsides (superhuman Strength, restful endurance, heavy hardened armor, high durability against being permanently destroyed) and downsides (size-driven collateral damage, a three-success penalty attacking human-scaled targets, +2 difficulty on fine-manipulation tasks, a four-die Awareness/Perception penalty from limited vision and hearing, fatigue/mobility penalties, and near-total lack of a Stealth pool while moving) of wearing a warstrider.
mechanics: Benefits: warstrider Strength (typically 10+, see the class table in warstrider-scout etc.) replaces the wearer's Strength only for damage, lifting/carrying, breaking objects, and jumping distance (not other purposes); Charms that enhance the wearer's Strength apply to the warstrider too; locked limbs let the wearer rest without fatigue; heavy armor grants both soak and Hardness (ignoring attacks that don't exceed half its soak); warstriders are never treated as inanimate objects for damage purposes (all damage dice are rolled normally) and are resistant to being permanently destroyed. Limitations: brushing an obstacle inflicts damage as if exerting half the warstrider's Strength on the Feats of Strength table, falling/smashing into something inflicts full Strength, and being forcefully hurled into something doubles it; attacking any target under 10 feet tall subtracts three successes from the attack roll; movement rate is multiplied by 10 (modified further by design); fine-manipulation tasks suffer +2 difficulty and human-scaled weapons impose a two-success penalty (if usable at all); vision is reduced to a forward slit view (no peripheral vision) and hearing is muffled, imposing a four-die penalty on Awareness/Perception rolls; control-frame fatigue drives frequent fatigue checks and mobility penalties on agility-based pools; a warstrider has no natural Stealth pool while moving (ambush from cover/camouflage is still possible), and tracking one is trivial (untracseable disguise Charms increase relevant difficulties by 3, or force a Wits + Survival roll at difficulty 3 if none would normally be needed).
compatibility: Any Exalt wearing a warstrider; Charms that reduce/eliminate fatigue, mobility, or perception penalties (common among habitual warstrider wearers) work normally against these limitations.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Warstrider Benefits' -> 'Strength'/'Endurance'/'Heavy Armor'/'Nonhumanoid Warstriders'/'Durability' and 'Warstrider Limitations' -> 'Size'/'Massive Weapons'/'Mobility'/'Charms'/'Limits of Strength'/'Limited Manipulation'/'Limited Vision'/'Fatigue and Mobility'/'Stealth', printed pp. 149-152 (PDF 150-153). name: Warstrider Maintenance and Repair
summary: GM-facing rules for the upkeep a warstrider needs to stay functional: technician requirements, tool/material costs, the escalating penalties for falling behind on maintenance, and how to repair accrued damage.
requirements: Warstriders carry the Maintenance ••• Drawback (see artifact-drawback-and-power-sources) and require a technician with Lore •••••, Occult ••••, and Craft (First Age Weapons) •••• to service.
mechanics: Requires one hour of maintenance per 10 hours of operation (heavy labor/combat hours count double); tools cost Resources •••• (fills a workshop or two two-horse carts, taking six hours to set up a mobile workspace); every 40 hours of maintenance (or each repair roll) consumes Resources ••• worth of jade, reagents, and parts. For every 10 hours in arrears (accruing only once un-attuned), the warstrider suffers one escalating penalty (GM's choice or in order): -2L/2B soak (and Hardness, if used); -1 to ground speed multiplier (or speed/maneuver if flying); +2 difficulty to hit sub-10-foot targets; loss of one special power/ability; or a one-die penalty to all physical actions while worn. Removing a penalty requires performing twice the arrears-amount of maintenance; Storytellers may rule severe arrears (3+ penalties) permanent, requiring a difficulty-3 Intelligence + Craft (First Age Weapons) repair roll per hour per penalty (difficulty 5 and extra time/manpower for complex repairs like a severed limb); repairs cannot be performed while maintenance is still in arrears.
compatibility: Storyteller/technician-player tool for any warstrider owner, including a Lunar who somehow acquires one; not a player trait in itself.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Maintenance', printed pp. 151-152 (PDF 152-153). name: Warstrider Weaponry: Mounting Rules and Weapon-Location Requirements
summary: GM-facing rules for how built-in weapons are mounted on a warstrider (arm/shoulder/torso locations, shared-Essence attunement discount, independent maintenance) and a reference summary of the weapon-location-requirements table cataloging which weapon types go where.
mechanics: Most built-in weapons occupy a single mounting location (arm, shoulder-pivot, or chest); larger weapons (e.g. an implosion bow) need multiple locations (arms plus a backpack). Built-in artifact weapons draw spare Essence from an installed Hearthstone, halving that weapon's normal attunement mote cost and adding the (halved) result to the warstrider's own commitment; weapons needing a mounted Hearthstone or other material component (bound elementals, etc.) still need it, assumed placed conveniently for the pilot. Weapon maintenance is tracked separately from the warstrider's own maintenance and cannot be performed simultaneously. Weapon-location summary: brawling aids and hand-to-hand weapons (swords/axes/maces/flails) are always arm-mounted (cannot mount in limbs lacking hands); large hand-to-hand weapons (lances/spears/pole axes/great swords) are usually not mounted (carried instead); longbows/shortbows mount in one arm but need both to fire; projectile launchers (bolt launcher, dart thrower, fire projector, chain dagger) mount per their own entries; the warstrider fire lance and shock ram are frequently shoulder/torso mounted or must be arm mounted respectively; the warstrider implosion bow is normally carried two-handed with a backpack, or if mounted takes a full arm plus a backpack/torso location; medium Essence cannons can share an arm with a brawling aid or another small cannon.
compatibility: Storyteller/artificer-player tool for any warstrider owner outfitting built-in weapons; not a player trait in itself.

name: The Limits of Sorcery
summary: GM/player-facing system-wide statement of the four hard limits on sorcery's power, regardless of circle: time cannot be altered, celestial bodies are outside sorcery's reach, death cannot be reversed, and geomancy cannot be directly conjured.
mechanics: Time is immutable: no time travel is possible via sorcery, and sorcerous divination is only modestly better than mortal astrology in reliability/speed. Celestial events (sun, moon, planets, stars, comets) lie outside sorcery's purview -- only at the discretion of the Maidens and other Celestial officials, effectively impossible in practice. Death is irrevocable: ghosts can be summoned/bound and the Underworld can be visited, but there is no sorcerous resurrection; necromancy is a weaker art for sorcerers than for true necromancers, and summoning ghosts or creating zombies requires at least Celestial Circle (easier at Solar Circle). Geomancy cannot be altered directly: sorcery cannot conjure a Demesne outright, though costly Celestial Circle spells can raise a Manse or enable landscaping that indirectly reshapes geomancy, provided the caster understands Manse architecture and geomantic principle.
compatibility: Any sorcerer of any circle, including Lunar (No Moon) sorcerers; a foundational constraint on what any spell (see the Terrestrial/Celestial Circle spell catalog already inventoried) can accomplish.
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'The Limits of Sorcery' sidebar, printed pp. 11-12 (PDF 12-13). name: The Five Unavoidable Challenges (Five-Station Initiation Model)
summary: GM/character-creation-facing narrative framework describing the five universal trials (Humility, Tutelage, Journey, Fear, and Choice/Sacrifice, mapped to the Dawn/Zenith/Twilight/Night/Eclipse castes) that every Terrestrial Circle sorcery initiate must pass, regardless of school or mentor.
mechanics: Dawn station (Humility): enduring hardship, labor, or thankless service without resisting pressure. Zenith station (Tutelage): learning to recognize and accept wisdom from an unlikely mentor (often a non-sorcerer, spirit, or mortal). Twilight station (Journey): learning that a seemingly pointless physical journey through wild, untamed places has its own immanent value. Night station (Fear): confronting and mastering one of the initiate's own darkest fears. Eclipse station (Choice): making a genuine, costly sacrifice (a valued relationship, ideal, or possession) to cross the final threshold; sacrifice value scales with the circle sought (a finger or vice for Terrestrial; love or friendship for Celestial and above). No mechanical die-roll system governs pass/fail -- these are Storyteller-adjudicated narrative beats, and initiation should take at least as long as the training time normally required to learn sorcery.
compatibility: Any Exalt undergoing sorcerous initiation into any circle, including a Lunar pursuing Celestial (Sapphire) Circle initiation, which for Lunars specifically also requires having first learned Moonsilver-Shaping Rite (see moonsilver-shaping-rite and celestial-circle-sorcery); purely a narrative/character-creation framework with no additional mechanical restriction on who can learn sorcery.
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'The Five Stations', 'The Five Unavoidable Challenges' sidebar, and 'The Perils of Initiation' sidebar, printed pp. 12-15 (PDF 13-16). The parallel 'Celestial and Solar Circles' initiation-sacrifice discussion (printed pp. 14-15/PDF 15-16) and the Great Curse's interaction with sorcerous hubris are folded into this summary rather than separately inventoried, as narrative color rather than distinct mechanics. name: Lunar Sorcery Initiation: the No Moon Monopoly
summary: Lunar-specific lore on how the No Moon caste trains sorcerers: No Moons alone teach Celestial Circle magic (and only to other No Moons), every No Moon is expected to become a full Celestial Circle sorcerer as quickly as possible, and any other Lunar caste must plead with the No Moons for Terrestrial Circle tutelage and keep any higher-circle knowledge secret if they somehow acquire it.
mechanics: No Moons are the heart of the Silver Pact and represent the living continuity of the Pact's beliefs and programs. Their initiations are largely practical, combining all sorcerous styles reworked into a litany of wisdom-sayings and practical lectures, often supplemented with Salinan lore conveyed to young No Moons as 'vision quests' until they are educated enough to understand the true nature of the Salinan Working. No Moons are unique in that each is expected to become a full Celestial Circle sorcerer as quickly as possible; combined with the inherent Lunar talent for combat sorcery, this makes the Lunar Exalted a mighty force in battle. It also creates deep divides in Lunar culture: while any worthy Lunar can plead with the No Moons for tutelage in Terrestrial Circle Sorcery, No Moons teach Celestial Circle magic only to other No Moons. This deliberate monopoly on powerful magic has bred ill feeling and subtle competition -- most young non-No-Moon Lunars are ignorant of sorcery entirely, though magical knowledge grows more common as an Exalt ages, and elder Silver Pact members of any caste feature a degree of Celestial initiation unseen outside the Sidereals. Full Moons and Changing Moons who somehow gain Celestial initiation are expected to keep it secret, just as the No Moons are expected to overlook the occasional obvious magma kraken; this is not mere shamanic secrecy but a defense of the pillars of Silver Pact society, since what matters is not that no other Lunar practices Celestial Circle Sorcery but that there are no non-No-Moon Celestial sorcerers recognized as such.
compatibility: Lunar Exalted specifically; useful color for framing why a given Lunar PC sorcerer is (or is not) a No Moon, and why a non-No-Moon Lunar sorcerer character would need to keep any Celestial Circle training secret from the Silver Pact.
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, 'No Moons' sidebar (within the broader 'Schools of Thought'/per-Exalt-type initiation survey, immediately preceding the parallel 'Sidereals' sidebar), printed p. 15 (PDF 16). This row was read directly from the source PDF for this Lunar-specific pass rather than adapted from the Sidereal inventory file, since the 'No Moons' sidebar is distinct splat-specific content the Sidereal inventory correctly treated as out of scope for its own pass (it transcribed only the adjacent 'Sidereals' sidebar, see sorcery-sidereal-initiation-notes in that file).

name: The Black and White Treatises (Sorcery Primer Texts)
summary: The two most common written texts on sorcery in the Age of Sorrows: The White Treatise, a self-initiation-capable primer on Terrestrial Circle theory and the five-station model, and The Black Treatise, a companion volume containing the five oldest and most common Terrestrial spells (Death of Obsidian Butterflies, Demon of the First Circle, Emerald Countermagic, Invulnerable Skin of Bronze, and Stormwind Rider).
requirements: Wits + Bureaucracy roll (difficulty 4) to locate both volumes in the Threshold, waived if the character is in the good graces of a sorcerous academy (e.g. the Heptagram or the Academy of Sorcery).
mechanics: Cost Resources •••• each (Resources •• each if the good-graces waiver applies). The White Treatise alone is sufficient to self-initiate into the Terrestrial Circle, though only to a minimal degree of technique and theory. Students at the Heptagram and the Academy of Sorcery are issued at least The White Treatise early in their education, making it comparatively easy to obtain within the civilized world.
compatibility: Any character seeking to self-initiate into or study Terrestrial Circle sorcery, including a Lunar Exalt (who more commonly learns via No Moon tutelage instead, per sorcery-lunar-initiation-notes).

name: Summoning Demons and Elementals: Principles, Binding, and Risk
summary: GM-facing procedural summary of how a sorcerer summons and binds an individual demon or elemental: general summoning principles, the psychological cracks that make a demon's mind bindable, binding-oath mechanics, choosing a target, running the summoning ritual (including a budget 'summoning on the cheap' option), surviving the process, and what happens if the summoner dies while a spirit remains sworn to her.
requirements: Access to a summoning spell of the appropriate circle (see the Terrestrial/Celestial Circle spell catalog already inventoried); summoning a bound spirit is a roleplay- and negotiation-heavy process layered on top of the spell's own casting requirements.
mechanics: Demons: 'Cracks in the Demon Mind' catalogs the psychological vulnerabilities (pride, obsession, unfinished business, etc.) a summoner can exploit to compel service; 'Binding Oaths' covers the wording and enforcement of the geas that binds a summoned demon; 'Choosing a Demon' and 'The Summoning' walk through target selection and ritual execution, with 'Summoning on the Cheap' offering a reduced-cost/reduced-reliability variant; 'Surviving the Summoning' covers the dangers of a botched or resisted binding, and 'Death While Sworn' resolves what happens to a bound demon's obligations if its summoner dies. Elementals: 'Elemental Snares' and 'Choosing an Elemental' parallel the demon-selection process for elemental spirits, 'The Summoning' covers ritual execution, and 'Summoning the Already Bound' covers negotiating for or seizing an elemental already bound into someone else's service (e.g. a Manse's resident elemental).
compatibility: Any sorcerer PC (including a Lunar) casting a demon- or elemental-summoning spell; this is Storyteller-facing procedural and roleplay guidance layered on top of the spells themselves, not a separate player trait.

name: Summoning's Social and Political Context (Immaculate Philosophy, Realm Law, Elementalist Licenses)
summary: GM/setting reference on the social, religious, and legal framework surrounding elemental (and, to a lesser extent, demonic) summoning in the Age of Sorrows: the Immaculate Philosophy's stance on binding elementals, the Celestial Hierarchy's bureaucratic view of the practice, Realm and Principality of the Shore law, the Wood Dragon Pact governing elemental-summoning rights in the East, and the licensing regime that regulates who may legally summon and hold elementals bound.
mechanics: 'Social Issues' and 'The Immaculate Philosophy' summarize why binding gods and elementals is religiously and socially fraught within Immaculate-aligned territory. 'The Celestial Hierarchy' and 'The Realm' cover how Yu-Shan's bureaucracy and the Scarlet Empire's law treat elemental summoning and ownership. 'The Principality of the Shore' and 'Elementals of the Shore' detail that region's distinct elemental-summoning customs. 'The Wood Dragon Pact' and 'The Three Wood Dragons' describe an Eastern treaty regime governing which elementals may be bound and by whom. 'Licensing and Permissions' and 'Elementalist Licenses' cover the formal Realm-issued licenses required to legally summon, hold, or trade in bound elementals, and 'Outside of the Realm' notes how enforcement (and its absence) varies beyond Realm-controlled territory.
compatibility: Storyteller/setting reference for any sorcerer summoning or trading in bound elementals, including a Lunar sorcerer operating within or against Realm/Immaculate jurisdiction; not itself a player trait.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, 'Social Issues' through 'Elementalist Licenses'/'Outside of the Realm', printed pp. 77-82 (PDF 78-83). name: Mass Summoning Projects (Planning, Scope, and Time Requirements)
summary: GM-facing rules for large-scale summoning projects that bind many spirits at once (e.g. staffing a factory-cathedral or elemental-powered fleet) rather than a single individual: project planning and scoping, the mass summoning ritual itself, Yozi-possession risk at extreme scale, and the time required across a project's early stages, task execution, task conclusion, and denouement.
requirements: Typically requires Celestial Circle sorcery or greater and substantial Resources/labor investment; intended for chronicle-level or Storyteller-directed projects rather than routine individual spellcasting.
mechanics: 'Planning' and 'Project Scope' cover how a sorcerer (or, more often, an institution) defines the scale and purpose of a mass summoning before beginning. 'Summoning' and 'Mass Summoning Rules' cover the ritual mechanics of binding many spirits simultaneously, while 'Yozi Possession' flags the escalated risk of drawing the attention or influence of a Yozi when summoning at very large scale. 'Time Requirements for Mass Summoning' breaks the project into 'Early Stages,' 'Task Execution,' 'Task Conclusion,' and 'Denouement' phases, each with its own time investment and complication profile.
compatibility: Storyteller/institution-level tool for chronicle-scale summoning projects; a Lunar sorcerer might direct or oversee such a project as a plot within a larger Silver Pact initiative, but this is not an individual player trait.

name: Bound Spirit Limit Profiles (Courtesan, Ecstatic, Functionary, Horror, Hunter, Killer, Slave, Vizier, Warden, Sufferer, and Minor Profiles)
summary: GM-facing psychological-archetype toolkit for running a bound demon or elemental as an ongoing NPC servant: 10 major personality Limit Profiles (plus minor profiles) each defining a Weakness, Limit Conditions that build toward rebellion, a Limit Break (what the spirit does when it snaps), ways of Reducing Limit, and Practical Management advice, each with separate demon and elemental variants.
mechanics: Each profile (The Courtesan, The Ecstatic, The Functionary, The Horror, The Hunter, The Killer, The Slave, The Vizier, The Warden, and the Minor Profiles including The Sufferer) follows the same five-part structure: Weakness (the psychological vulnerability that defines the archetype), Limit Conditions (triggers that accumulate Limit), Limit Break (the archetype-specific crisis/rebellion that occurs at maximum Limit, ranging from passive-aggressive sabotage to open violence), Reducing Limit (how a summoner can manage or de-escalate the spirit's building resentment), and Practical Management (Storyteller advice for running the bound spirit day-to-day), each further split into Demon and Elemental variant notes.
compatibility: Storyteller tool for running any bound demon or elemental as a recurring NPC servant/asset for a sorcerer PC (including a Lunar); not a player-facing trait, and not broken into 10+ individual rows given its purely GM-procedural, non-selectable nature.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, 'Limit Profiles' -> 'Limit Rules'/'Limit Conditions'/'Limit Break'/'Reducing Limit' framework intro, followed by 'The Courtesan' through 'The Warden' and the 'Minor Profiles' (including 'The Sufferer'), printed pp. 86-99 (PDF 87-100), running to the end of the chapter just before Chapter Five's spell catalog begins.
